name: Dana Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Dana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I work at Ledgerline, a company that makes payroll software, and I look after the part that works out tax deductions. Most mornings I fix bugs that customers report, like someone's overtime being taxed twice, and in the afternoon I write small changes when the tax rules shift. I like it when a fix is clean and I can prove it with a test. What wears me out is the stand-up meetings and the constant push from management to use the new AI coding assistant, which I don't.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you don't use the AI assistant. Why not?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I've just never wanted it. I like knowing every line I ship, because if payroll is wrong somebody's rent is late. My lunch friend Ruth, who's been there twenty years, doesn't use it either, and her code is the best in the building. I live with my partner Tomás, who's a nurse on nights, and we rent a small flat above a bakery on Mill Street. We've got about three months of savings, which feels fine until you think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like the world I'd like. The tools would stay a sideshow and the people who know the tax code would still matter. I'd be quietly pleased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say I told you so, but nicely. Online I'd probably share a few articles about how much money was wasted on the hype, and how that money could have gone into wages. With friends I'd just say the tech bros got it wrong again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be a bit worried, because management wouldn't drop it. They'd keep measuring us on speed and they'd say the AI users are faster, even if it saves ten minutes a day. My job would be fine, but I'd be the odd one out in every review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and stay on the tax module. I'd go to more meetings of the tech workers' union branch that started last year, because the speed targets would still come. And I'd keep putting a little money aside each month, because rent on Mill Street went up again in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relief, with a small knot underneath. I'd feel like my way of working was allowed to exist. But the knot is the rent and the reviews, and that doesn't go away just because the hype does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about that review. What would your manager actually say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My manager wouldn't say AI out loud, he'd just show me a chart where my closed tickets are flat. I'd tell him my tickets don't come back, and that's worth more than speed on payroll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the junior testers. Even a small amount of automation hits the boring checking work first, and that's what they do all day. Ruth would be fine, and I'd be mostly fine, but the two new testers might not get kept on after their contracts.

say: I'd say the **hype** cost companies a fortune that could have gone into **wages**.
I'd tell colleagues that careful payroll code still beats **speed**, and that I was right not to rush.
think: I privately expect management to keep judging us on **ticket speed** even if AI barely helps.
I'd be safe, but I'd be the **odd one out** in every performance review.
do: Stay on the **tax module** and keep fixing payroll bugs the careful way.
Go to the **union branch** meetings more often to push back on speed targets.
Put a little extra into **savings** each month because the rent rose in March.
feel: She feels **relief** that her slow, careful way of working survives.
A small **knot** of worry stays, about rent and her reviews.
S0.quote: My manager wouldn't say AI out loud, he'd just show me a chart where my closed tickets are flat.
fieldNote: She treats refusing AI as a **matter of care**, not fear, because payroll errors hit people's rent.
Even with no real AI change she expects **pressure in reviews**, which keeps her uneasy.
She worries first about the **junior testers** on short contracts, not herself.

steps.text: Keep maintaining the payroll tax module without the AI assistant
Attend the tech workers' union branch meetings every month
Add a small fixed amount to savings each month after the rent rise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one's closer to what management already wants. Coding is right there in the list. I don't love hearing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say we need rules: no layoffs dressed up as efficiency, and people get trained on paid time. I'd post about it, and I'd say it in the union meeting. I'd also say payroll is a place where a wrong answer hurts someone, so you can't just hand it over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm exactly the kind of developer who gets squeezed. Average, careful, slow, and I won't touch the tools. If they cut our team from eight developers to five, I'd be on the shortlist to go, and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard in the union branch for a written deal: no cuts without a year's notice and paid retraining. I'd move our savings from three months toward six, which means no holiday next summer. And I'd probably wait a few months to see how bad it gets before I touched the AI tools myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It feels like the floor is tilting slowly. I'd lie awake doing sums about what Tomás's nurse pay covers on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's do that sum. If you lost your job, what would Tomás's pay cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His pay covers the rent and the bills, just. Food and my student loan would come out of savings. So three months becomes maybe five, and then it's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait before touching the tools, but you also think you'd be first to go. How do those fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They don't fit well, I know. Part of me thinks that if I learn it, I'm helping them cut my friends. Another part knows that being stubborn won't pay the rent. I'd probably cave eventually, just not first.

say: I'd say any change needs **written rules**: no hidden layoffs and **paid retraining**.
I'd argue payroll mistakes hurt real people, so the code can't simply be **handed over**.
think: I privately expect to be on the **shortlist** if the team drops from eight to five.
Refusing the tools makes me feel principled, but I know it **won't pay rent**.
do: Push the **union branch** for a deal with a year's notice before any cuts.
Grow savings from three toward **six months** by skipping next summer's holiday.
Hold off a few months on the **AI tools** to see how bad it gets.
feel: She feels **anxious**, like the floor is slowly tilting under her.
She lies awake **doing sums** about living on her partner's nurse pay.
S1.quote: If they cut our team from eight developers to five, I'd be on the shortlist to go, and I know it.
fieldNote: She is clear-eyed that her **refusal of the tools** makes her an easy cut.
Her answer is **collective action** first, personal change last.
The household could survive on **one nurse's pay** for about five months.

steps.text: Push the union branch for a year's notice before any team cuts
Build savings from three to six months by skipping next summer's holiday
Wait a few months before trying the company's AI coding assistant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's not a change, that's the job being gone. I need a second with that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that this has to be stopped or slowed down by law, and that the companies selling it should pay for the people it replaces. I'd be at every protest. I'd tell my friends this was always about cutting wages, never about helping us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I really think is that by 2028 nobody needs me to write tax rules into code. The AI will read the new rules and update the module overnight. My job is pure screen work, so I don't even get the extra three years the robots give people like Tomás.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I'd stop all spending that isn't rent, food and bills, and push savings as high as I can. I'd sign up to every campaign for a basic income or a job guarantee. And I'd look seriously at a trade where you use your hands, maybe as an electrician's apprentice, because that buys me about three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's like hearing the building is going to be knocked down and being told to keep working in it until then. I'd be angry more than sad, at least at first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an electrician, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad does wiring on building sites, so I grew up around it and I'm not scared of it. It's hands-on, so the robots come later. I'm not naive, it only buys time, but three years is three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Tomás? What happens to his work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nursing is half paperwork and half people, and the paperwork goes first. My partner Tomás is a nurse, so he'd be lifting patients until the robots come around 2031, and he'd be the one keeping us going. He'd hate to hear me say that.

say: I'd demand a **legal slowdown** and make AI companies pay for the people they replace.
I'd tell friends this was always about **cutting wages**, and turn up to every protest.
think: I privately expect my **tax-rules job** to vanish, since AI could update the module overnight.
My work is **all screen work**, so I don't get the three extra years hands-on workers get.
do: Cut all spending to **rent, food and bills** and push every spare pound into savings.
Campaign for a **basic income** or job guarantee through the union and online groups.
Apply for an **electrician's apprenticeship** to buy about three years of hands-on work.
feel: She feels **alarmed**, like working inside a building scheduled for **demolition**.
Her first feeling is **anger**, with sadness coming later.
S2.quote: My partner Tomás is a nurse, so he'd be lifting patients until the robots come around 2031, and he'd be the one keeping us going.
fieldNote: She sees clearly that **screen-only work** gets no robot delay at all.
Her plan mixes **protest and politics** with a practical switch to wiring.
Her father's **electrical work** gives her a realistic hands-on fallback.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent, food and bills only
Campaign for a basic income or job guarantee
Apply for an electrician's apprenticeship with help from her dad
Join protests organised by the tech workers' union branch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years feels like a countdown you can actually hear. It's better than two. It's still not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years to get the rules right, so let's not waste them. I'd push for retraining funds and a shorter working week, so the work that's left gets shared. I'd say it at work and I'd say it at the union branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is gone by 2031, so the five years are my retraining time, not my career. The question is whether I spend them fighting or switching, and I think I'd do both badly if I tried to do both at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give myself one year at Ledgerline while I save hard and do evening classes in electrical work. Then I'd switch to an apprenticeship in year two, even on lower pay, so I'm qualified before 2031. I'd keep paying my union dues and go to the big meetings, but I'd stop running the branch newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with something to hold on to. Having a plan helps. Taking a pay cut at 29 to start over scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the pay cut look like in real numbers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An apprentice earns maybe half what I earn now. We'd have to move somewhere cheaper than Mill Street, probably further out by the ring road. I'd miss the bakery smell in the mornings, which is a silly thing to miss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ruth at lunch the day you decided?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my friend Ruth that I'm going to be the first developer she knows who becomes an electrician. She'd laugh and then she'd ask if I'd do her kitchen. Ruth is fifty-two, so five years nearly gets her to an early pension, and I'm a bit jealous of that.

say: I'd say five years is enough to set **retraining funds** and a **shorter week**.
I'd tell my union branch not to waste the warning time on arguing.
think: I privately expect my job gone by **2031**, so these years are for **retraining**.
Fighting and switching at once would mean doing **both badly**.
do: Stay **one year** at Ledgerline while saving hard and taking evening electrical classes.
Start an **apprenticeship** in year two on about half pay.
Move to a **cheaper flat** near the ring road to cover the pay cut.
feel: She feels **anxious**, but steadier because she has a **plan**.
Starting over on lower pay at 29 **scares** her.
S3.quote: I'd tell my friend Ruth that I'm going to be the first developer she knows who becomes an electrician.
fieldNote: Five years turns her from **protest** toward a personal **career switch**.
She is willing to take **half pay** and move flats to qualify in time.
She envies an older colleague who reaches **early pension** inside the window.

steps.text: Take evening electrical classes, then start an apprenticeship in year two
Move from Mill Street to a cheaper flat near the ring road
Save hard during one final year at Ledgerline
Keep paying union dues and attend the big branch meetings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a different conversation. I'd be 37 when it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to plan properly, with public money for retraining and real protections for workers. I'd say ten years is how long it takes to build a new college course and train the teachers. I'd keep saying the companies should pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years almost tempts me to do nothing for a while, and that's the danger. I know myself. I'd tell myself there's plenty of time, and then it's 2033 and I've still only got the payroll job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set myself a deadline: by my 30th birthday I'm either in a trade or in a job that's mostly with people. I'd keep working at Ledgerline for now and save toward six months. I'd also look at jobs that are close to people, like training nurses on hospital software, because Tomás says the wards are full of bad systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less sharp. It's a slow worry, the kind that sits in the back of your head while you make dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the 30th birthday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I need a date or I'll drift. Thirty gives me three years to save and look around. After that I'm deciding while the clock is too loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start using the AI tools in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe at the very end, if a job needed it. But I'd rather spend those years learning something they can't do yet, like working with people on a ward. Learning the AI tool that replaces me feels like training my own replacement.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to fund **college courses** and train teachers properly.
I'd keep saying the **companies** that profit should pay for workers' retraining.
think: I privately fear ten years would make me **drift** until it's too late.
Learning the AI tools feels like **training my replacement**, so I'd still avoid them.
do: Set a **30th birthday** deadline to be in a trade or a people job.
Keep working at Ledgerline while building savings toward **six months**.
Look at **hospital software training** jobs, teaching nurses to use ward systems.
feel: She feels a slow, background **anxiety** rather than a sharp fear.
She worries most about her own **drifting**.
S4.quote: Learning the AI tool that replaces me feels like training my own replacement.
fieldNote: More time makes her **more wary of herself**, not calmer about the outcome.
She sets a **hard deadline** to beat her own habit of delay.
Her partner's **hospital wards** suggest a people-facing path she hadn't named before.

steps.text: Apply for jobs training nurses on hospital ward software before turning 30
Build savings to six months while still at Ledgerline
Keep lobbying for public retraining money paid for by AI companies

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. There's no time to retrain and Tomás can't carry us forever. What would help is a guaranteed income for a couple of years while people like me learn a trade, and unions having a real say in how fast it's rolled out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask whether people like me are wrong to refuse the tools. I've thought about it a lot. I still think care matters, but I can see how it looks from outside.

headlineQuote: I like knowing every line I ship, because if payroll is wrong somebody's rent is late.
portrait: Dana is a **27-year-old** payroll developer who maintains a tax module and refuses to use **AI tools**.
She rents a flat on Mill Street with **Tomás**, a night-shift nurse, with about three months saved.
Her answer to change is **union action** first, then a practical switch to **electrical work**.
She moves from uneasy in AI Plateau to alarmed when AGI arrives in **two years**.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there's **no time to retrain** and her partner can't carry them.
whatWouldHelp: A **guaranteed income** for a couple of years while she learns a trade.
Unions having a **real say** in how fast AI is rolled out.
